set.approach: In winter the road is plowed only part of the way, so the trip to Granite Lake is a long ski or walk of roughly 9 to 10 miles, first up the snow-covered road to the trailhead and then along the trail beside Granite Creek. Most parties camp in the trees at the north end of the lake. Cross the lake to its south shore and head up the snow gully beneath the Thunderdome buttress; the lines hang on the wall above. Avalanche terrain is present, so check the avalanche forecast. Bartertown is the lone large sheet of ice on the far right side of the buttress; it is the line that catches the eye when you look up from the lake.
set.descent_text: Three finishes top out the route; the left-hand one has a good tree for a rappel anchor a short way above the lip, and parties rappel from there.

set.approach: Follow the maintained Sphinx Mountain trail, roughly 4.5 to 5.5 miles, to the high saddle between the Sphinx and the Helmet; there is a campsite in the trees at the saddle. From the saddle, climb the ridge above it for a few hundred feet until a break in the cliff band lets you traverse left toward the north face, and the ice becomes visible as you round the corner. The gullies on the way carry avalanche hazard, so check the avalanche forecast, and allow more time than the distance suggests. The Lowe Route is the left-hand of the three main ice lines in the middle of the face.
set.descent_text: A couloir above the last ice leads to the summit ridge, and broken ridge scrambling then reaches the summit. Go down the nontechnical northwest face to the saddle, or take the bowl to the skier's right, where a path branches off about three-quarters of the way down toward the ridge used on the way in. Nothing is harder than third class.

review.notes: Route page for the line and its descent; the saddle approach and the walk-off down the northwest face agree with the trip report and the area page.

set.descent_text: From the top of the face, continue to the summit or descend into the large bowl to the skier's right. About three-quarters of the way down the bowl, a path leads off to skier's right toward the ridge used on the way in and the saddle. The terrain is nontechnical, and bearing right keeps you on line.

review.notes: Route page for position beside the Lowe Route, the traverse approach and the descent; saddle and trail from the area page and trip report.

set.approach: Start from the Ashley Lakes trailhead. Either grind straight uphill to above the trees, where the technical ground starts, or walk the Ashley Lakes trail to the first lake, leave it there, and angle up the drainage's north (left) side. The route follows the west ridge, which holds snow gendarmes and large cornices, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the route along the west ridge, then return to the Ashley Lakes trail and walk out.

review.notes: Route page for trailhead, the two ways up to the ridge and the descend-the-route statement; the Ashley Lakes access and ridge character from the two trip accounts. No distances given.

set.approach: Leave the car at Lake Macdonald, continue along the trail beyond the lake, then swing south over the creek and ascend the nameless drainage that ends beneath the north face. The approach is a hard bushwhack. The face carries cornices on the summit ridge above, which is why parties start early.
set.descent_text: Two ways down are used. One option runs down the west ridge to Ashley Lakes and out that trail, which suits a party that has left a car at that trailhead. The alternative is the east ridge down to the low point linking Sheepshead with Macdonald Peak, followed by the approach drainage back out.

review.notes: Route's own page for approach and both descents; west ridge page confirms the Ashley Lakes trailhead walk-out. Distances and times left out because only one source gives them.

set.approach: Start at the Carpp Creek trailhead and hike the Upper Carpp Lake trail, going on up to Warren Pass. From the pass, bear southwest past the last trees toward a small tarn; the couloir is obvious above it. The tarn is frozen in early season. The couloir is steep snow, so check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Usually descend by downclimbing the steep couloir until the slope eases enough to glissade, depending on conditions. The rocky ridges from the summit are another option, with care on loose, exposed rock.

review.notes: Route page for approach line and descent options; the area page confirms the Upper Carpp Lake and Warren Pass approach.
